Gallium nitride ( GaN) travel chargers, however, offer a more convenient solution. GaN travel chargers have interchangeable sockets for use in different countries. They plug directly into wall sockets and can rapidly charge multiple devices simultaneously.
 And since they are compatible with UK wall sockets, they can be used in Singapore so users don’t need to buy an extra charger. One charger that will rule them all? It’s a small slice of nerd heaven that I’d gladly sign up for.

 WHAT TO LOOK FOR IN A GAN TRAVEL CHARGER 
 Gallium nitride (GaN) is a semiconductor that conducts electricity more efficiently and generates less heat than silicon-based chargers. This allows them to charge multiple devices faster and have more compact designs. 
 Sockets: Check that your travel charger includes US, EU, AU and UK sockets so you’re covered wherever you travel in the world. 
 Power output: If you want to fast-charge your laptop, or charge your phone and laptop simultaneously, consider a charger that supports at least 65W charging. 
 Size, weight and cost: The current GaN charger sweet spot lies with 65W and 100W devices. More powerful chargers will be bigger, heavier and in some case, much more expensive. If you travel with a lot of devices that need to be charged rapidly, this could still be a viable option for you. 
 Safety: Look for built-in features like over-voltage, over-current and short-circuit protection that help protect your devices.

The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom.  Travel Adapters: Your Questions, Answered
 What Type of Adapter Do You Need?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 There are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.
 Type A and Type B are used in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Japan.
 Type C is common across Europe, South America, and Asia.
 Type E and Type F are found across Europe in places like Germany, Russia, and France.
 Type G is used in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and a handful of other places.
 Type I is used in Australia, New Zealand, China, and Argentina.
 Some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India ( Type D ), Israel ( Type H ), and South Africa ( Type M or N ). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.
 If you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.
 Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Photograph: Simon Hill 
 Voltage converters are big, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:
 Input: 100–220V 50/60Hz 
 That should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. Most places provide hair dryers , irons, and kettles , so there’s no need to take them with you. It’s also often cheaper to buy a set with the correct plug at your destination and save the luggage space and hassle.
 If you are determined to try a voltage converter (again, I don’t recommend doing so), the Ceptics 2,000-watt Travel Voltage Converter ($70) seems to work well. It has a special 2,000-watt outlet for hair dryers, but only ones that work via a mechanical switch (anything with an electronic circuit board for automatic switch-off or temperature control won’t work and is at risk of being fried if plugged in). It also has two outlets that go up to 200 watts, one USB-C port, and three USB-A ports, though the ports do not support fast charging.
 What About Wattage?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Travel adapters and chargers usually state the wattage they can deliver for USB-C and USB-A ports, retractable cables, and wireless charging. If you're interested in getting the fastest rates possible, you’ll want a charger and cable that can deliver the maximum wattage to your device. A laptop might want 100 watts, while a phone only needs 30 watts. There's no need to worry if the charger can deliver more wattage than is required because the device will dictate how much power to draw. If the wattage is lower than required, most devices will simply charge slowly. You can find out more about charging standards like Power Delivery (PD), Quick Charge (QC), and others in my guide on how to fast charge your phone .
 Can Travel Adapters Go in a Suitcase?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Yes, you can pack travel adapters in your suitcase . It may be wise to bring one in your hand luggage for easy access should you need to charge up a device when you arrive at your destination. In fact, devices like power banks with lithium batteries (must be capped at 27,000 mAh ) must go in hand luggage, not checked bags .
 Can I Buy Travel Adapters at the Airport or Hotel?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 You certainly can buy travel adapters at the airport, but like all other goods you buy at kiosks between connecting flights, they will be far more expensive than necessary, and your choice will be limited.
 Some hotels have travel adapters, and some even have wall outlets for other countries (or USB-A and USB-C ports), but most do not, so don’t bank on it. You can always check with your hotel or accommodation before you depart, but it’s safer to bring a travel adapter with you.
 Should You Test Your Travel Adapter Before You Go?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Seriously, nothing is worse than thinking you’re being very clever by packing light only to get to your hotel and discover that your gadgets refuse to charge. Between the adapter, cable, and your device, plenty can go wrong, so do a quick test on your wall outlet at home with everything you are taking before you set off on an international trip.
 How I Test Travel Adapters
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 Anytime I fly for work or vacation, I take a few travel adapters and chargers with me to test. I also test them for longer periods at home in the UK. I have power stations and power strips with US and EU outlets to test those plugs. I test each charger with a variety of devices (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, MacBook, AirPods). I try charging with every port and outlet simultaneously to see if the charger gets warm. I assess the charging rates, durability, size, weight, and usability of each device. If there are any special features, I test them too.
 More Travel Adapters I Like
 There are many travel adapters out there. These are a few others I tested and liked, but they missed out on a place above for one reason or another.
 Photograph: Simon Hill 
 Epicka Pulse for $27 : The beveled edges of this travel adapter from Epicka make it more comfortable to hold. The sliders work well and lock in place securely to cover you in around 200 countries. A pair of USB-C and two USB-A ports provide a good mix of port options. This adapter can deliver up to 45 watts from either USB-C port, while the USB-A ports top out at 18 watts. I also tested the newer Epicka Pulse Duo ($130) , which can deliver up to 140 watts across three USB-C and one USB-A ports, has an extra US or Japanese socket in the side and boasts a smart display that shows you the current charging status, wattage, and temperature. Cool as it is, it's overkill for most folks and kinda pricey.
 Tessan Travel Adapter 009 for $17 : This is a similar design to the Epicka Air I recommend above, but the prongs don’t stay in place as securely when unfolded, and you can only draw a maximum of 20 watts from the one USB-A and two USB-C ports. But it is affordable and compact. Tessan also makes good, traditional, slider universal adapters: There's a 140-watt model ($70) , and the most powerful travel adapter I’ve tested, the Voyager 205 ($128) , which has six USB-C ports and one USB-A to deliver up to 205 watts. If you don’t care about charging speed, Tessan's 20W model ($29) is very reasonably priced and offers two USB-A and two USB-C ports in a small package.
 Photograph: Simon Hill 
 UGreen Travel Plug Adapter for £17 : This travel adapter is for UK folks visiting Europe, and it’s a solid option with a fixed plug (no mechanism). It has only two USB-A and one USB-C port for smaller devices, and it’s very bulky. I prefer the OneBeat above for this type of design.
 Statik SmartCharge Pro for $80 : This is a nice combo device that includes a 15,000 mAh power bank and a 60-watt wall charger. There are fold-out US prongs and slide-on adapters for the UK, EU, and AU. You also get one USB-A port, one USB-C port, a fold-out USB-C cable, and a wireless charging pad on top that works with your iPhone or Apple Watch.
 D-Link 65W Multi-Port GaN Charger (DCP-651) for $40 : If two USB-C ports and a USB-A port are enough for your travel needs, this affordable D-Link charger could be for you. It comes with interchangeable plugs for different countries. The 65-watt limit is enough for overnight charging a laptop and a couple of smartphones.
 Arsmel VisaPro
 Photograph: Simon Hil 
 Arsmel VisaPro All-in-One Travel Adapter for $80 : This chunky power adapter can charge laptops or multiple small devices with a whopping 170-watt maximum output. It works with any outlet in the US, UK, or EU, thanks to sliding plugs that slot in securely, and you can spin the prongs on the US plug to support the total number of countries (more than 200). I love the mecha-inspired paint job, too. There are four ports along the bottom: two USB-C ports rated at 140 watts, with the third USB-C and USB-A ports rated at 18 watts. It supports PD 3.1, QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and SCP, and has a 10-amp fuse.
 Satechi GaN Travel Charger for $120 : If you only take small gadgets with you when you travel, a compact, multi-port wall charger is all you need and a great way to pack light. It plugs directly into the wall and comes with four interchangeable travel adapters for the EU, UK, and Australia, plus a mesh bag to store them. There are four USB-C ports that you can plug your gadgets into, including laptops like the MacBook Pro, tablets, phones, and wearables. With support for Power Delivery 3.1, the first two ports can supply up to 140 watts, and the bottom two ports up to 45 watts. However, the maximum output when all four ports are in use is 145 watts.
 Baseus 70W Universal Travel Adapter With Retractable Cable for $40 : This excellent travel adapter is almost identical to our top pick from Ceptics, offering up to 70 watts, sliding prongs to cover more than 200 countries, and a built-in retractable USB-C cable, not to mention a USB-C port and two USB-A ports. It also has a snazzy black-and-yellow finish. It only misses out because it’s slightly more expensive, but if you can snag one on sale or prefer the colors, it’s a solid option.
 Epicka Universal Travel Adapter for $20 : This travel adapter from Epicka is still a solid option. The sliding plugs cover 150 countries, and there are four USB-A ports on the bottom and a 15-watt USB-C port on the side. There’s also an 8-amp fuse with a spare, and this adapter is RoHS-, CE-, and FCC-certified.
 Masterplug Visitor to UK Travel Adapter (3 Pack) for £12 : For visitors to the UK, this simple trio of adapters accepts European, American, Australian, and Asian plugs. They are single-outlet adapters with 13-amp fuses inside, and they work perfectly. These are the adapters I use for long-term testing of devices from the US and elsewhere that lack UK plugs. If you forgot to buy an adapter before arriving in the UK, you can find this affordable three-pack at any Argos store.
 Anker European Travel Plug Adapter for $16 : One of our favorite portable charger brands, Anker, also makes travel adapters. This one plugs into most European outlets to provide a single grounded US outlet, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. Unfortunately, the three USB ports max out at 15 watts total, so it’s best for overnight gadget charging, but I appreciate the temperature and overload protection. There is also a UK version ($16) .
 Epicka Hybrid European Travel Plug Adapter for $20 : This handy adapter turns one outlet into four and includes four USB ports (two A and two C). It has fold-out Type A prongs, but you can also slide on a fold-out Type C plug for use in Europe. While the USB ports support QC 3.0 or PD 3.0, they max out at 20 watts in total. I prefer the OneBeat adapters recommended above.

 You can do better than these travel adapters.
 EZQuest WorldTravel
 Photograph: Simon Hill 
 EZQuest WorldTravel GaN 5 Port With PD Wall Charger : This travel adapter has a generous four USB-C ports and one USB-A port with a familiar slide-out prong design that covers more than 150 countries. There’s also a built-in 10-amp fuse and a spare. It has RoHS, CE, and FCC certification. It works fine, but it's kinda boxy, and the sliders don't lock in place as securely as some of our other picks. There's also a 65W version ($60) .
 Rolling Square Pocket Travel Adapter : I admire any attempt to shrink down travel adapters in size, but the three-pronged UK plugs are usually the obstacle. Rolling Square’s solution is to have a flip-out third prong, but you’ll need a good fingernail to unhitch it. This charger has a single USB-C port capable of delivering up to 30 watts and is a compact option that covers the US, UK, and Europe.
 Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter
 Photograph: Simon Hill 
 Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter : This versatile adapter comes with Type A, B, C, E/F, G, and I slide-on plugs. They fit onto the rectangular brick and plug directly into the outlet, or you can attach them to the optional five-foot cable. The brick has one grounded US outlet and a second non-grounded outlet, with one USB-A (30-watt) and two USB-C (65- and 33-watt) ports at the other end. It works fine, and it's affordable, but it's bulky and ugly.

 Which wattage for which device Wattage Best for Our pick

The exception is the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which Apple says charge fastest on a 60W-capable adapter or higher that supports USB PD 3.2 AVS.
 For a laptop and a phone together, 65W is the sweet spot. It fast-charges a MacBook Air and keeps a phone topped up from the same plug.
 For a 14 or 16-inch MacBook Pro under sustained load, step up to 100W. Above that you are no longer buying for one laptop, you are buying for two, or for a whole desk of devices.
 Best 30W GaN charger: Anker 511 Nano 4. A phone fast-charges at 20 to 30W and will not go faster on a bigger charger, so for a phone-only bag the Nano 4 at about 90g is all you need.
 Best 65W GaN charger: UGREEN Nexode Pro 65W. The tier most travelers should buy. How-To Geek confirmed 65W from one port, and ChargerLab records a 45W and 20W split with two devices, enough for a MacBook Air and a phone in a 113g body. The budget answer in this tier is the Baseus 65W 3-Port.

 Alisdair’s answer: think about the biggest single thing you plug in, and buy for that. Nothing else on the box matters much.
 Only a phone? The little 30W is all you will ever use. A laptop and a phone? The 65W does both from one outlet.
 A big work laptop that runs hot all day is the 100W. Everything above that is for charging two laptops, or a whole desk, at once.

 GaN is short for gallium nitride, a semiconductor that replaces silicon in the part of a charger that chops wall power into the low voltage your devices take. It can switch on and off far faster than silicon and stand much higher voltages.
 The reason is the material itself. Gallium nitride has a bandgap of 3.4 electron volts against silicon’s 1.1, which is why IEEE Spectrum calls it the ideal semiconductor for power-hungry electronics.
 In a wall charger that translates into three things you can feel: fewer and smaller parts inside, less energy wasted as heat at every switch, and a block that ends up far smaller than the brick your laptop shipped with.

 GaN versus silicon, in practice. A silicon charger of the same wattage needs a bigger transformer and a bigger heatsink, so it is heavier and warmer for the same output. GaN does not make a charger magic; it moves the point at which heat becomes a problem.
 Heat and throttling. That point still exists. In Tom’s Hardware’s 30 minute test all three 140W chargers cut their output after 15 minutes as they heated up, the best of them settling at 118W with a surface reading of 67 degrees C, and a 100W Anker Prime slipped from 99W to 89W.
 Every charger in the 45 to 68W band held full output for the whole run. That is the engineering reason a 65W block is the right buy for one laptop and a phone, and why the 100W and 200W picks here are for people running two laptops or a desk.
 GaN generations. You will see GaN 3, GaN 4 and GaN 5 on boxes, and UGREEN numbers its own. Later generations push higher wattage into the same size, but the label is marketing; the numbers that matter are the per-port wattage and whether the charger holds it once warm.
 Safety marks. A genuine GaN charger carries a safety certification against IEC 62368-1: UL or ETL in the US, UKCA in the UK, CE in the EU. Counterfeits sold under unknown names leave out the thermal cut-out and the insulation barrier that standard requires, and they weigh noticeably less than the real thing.
 Buy from the brand’s own store or its official Amazon storefront, and treat a 65W GaN charger at a fraction of the usual weight as the warning sign it is.

 Do I still need a travel adapter with a GaN charger? Yes, in most cases. GaN chargers sold on Amazon UK, Amazon.de and Amazon.com ship with a single regional plug, and the charger itself runs on any voltage from 100 to 240V, so it is only the plug that stops working abroad.

 Can a 65W GaN charger replace my laptop’s original charger? For most laptops, yes. A MacBook Air charges at up to 67W over USB-C, so a 65W GaN charger fast-charges it about as effectively as the original.
 A 14 or 16-inch MacBook Pro can accept 96W to 140W. On 65W it will charge, but under heavy use it may not recover faster than the battery drains, so 100W is the safer choice for a high-performance laptop.
 Does wattage drop when charging multiple devices at once? Yes. Multi-port chargers split their total wattage across the active ports, so the UGREEN Nexode Pro 65W delivers 65W to one device but records a 45W and 20W split with two connected.
 That is how shared power budgets work rather than a flaw. The number to check is the primary-port output when all ports are in use, not the single-port maximum on the box.
 Are GaN chargers allowed on planes and in a carry-on? Yes. Wall chargers have no watt-hour restriction on commercial flights, because the 100Wh airline battery rule applies only to lithium batteries, meaning portable power banks rather than plug-in chargers. A GaN wall charger can travel in your carry-on or checked baggage on any commercial flight.
 What is the difference between GaN, GaN5, GaNInfinity and GaNPrime? GaN is the core technology, gallium nitride transistors that run more efficiently than silicon, and GaN5 is the fifth generation of it, running cooler than earlier designs. GaNInfinity from UGREEN and GaNPrime from Anker are each brand’s current-generation chip name, both indicating improved thermal management over standard GaN5. The generation matters; the brand name is secondary.
 Is 65W or 100W better for a MacBook Air? 65W is right for a MacBook Air. It charges at up to 67W over USB-C or MagSafe 3, so a 65W GaN charger matches Apple’s own adapter, and the 100W pick is there for MacBook Pro users or a higher-wattage Windows laptop.
 Is a GaN charger a good iPhone charger? Yes. A GaN charger makes an excellent iPhone charger because it uses USB-C Power Delivery, far faster than an old 5W plug. For an iPhone on its own the Anker 511 Nano 4 at 30W is plenty for most models, though an iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max charges fastest on a 60W-capable adapter with USB PD 3.2 AVS; for an iPhone plus a laptop from one plug, the UGREEN Nexode Pro 65W is the pick.
 Can a GaN charger charge a Chromebook or laptop? Yes. A USB-C GaN charger doubles as a Chromebook and laptop charger, because almost every Chromebook, Windows ultrabook and MacBook now charges over USB-C Power Delivery. Most thin laptops run on 45W to 65W; for a 14 or 16-inch MacBook Pro or a gaming laptop, step up to the Anker Prime 100W or the Anker 4-Port 140W.
 Will a GaN charger overheat my phone or laptop? No. GaN chargers run cooler than the older silicon designs they replace, because gallium nitride wastes less energy as heat, and every pick here negotiates power with your device over USB Power Delivery so the device only draws what it asks for. Independent load testing on these picks reported no overheating under sustained use.
 What is USB Power Delivery and why does it matter for travel? USB Power Delivery, usually shortened to PD, is the standard that lets a charger and a device agree how much power to move between them. It is what allows one small charger to fast-charge a phone at 30W and a laptop at 100W from the same port.
 For travel it matters because a single PD charger replaces the separate bricks you would otherwise carry, and PD 3.1 pushes that ceiling up to 140W for high-wattage laptops. The USB Implementers Forum, the standards body behind PD, publishes the full specification on its USB charger and PD page .
 What is the lightest GaN travel charger in this roundup? The Anker 511 Nano 4 at about 90g, though it is a single-port 30W phone charger. If you need a laptop covered as well, the lightest capable pick is the UGREEN Nexode Pro 65W at 113g, which adds two more ports and enough output for a MacBook Air.
 What is the best USB-C charger for an iPhone or Android phone? For a phone on its own, the Anker 511 Nano 4 at 30W is the sensible choice, because most current iPhones and Android phones fast-charge at 20 to 30W and will not go faster on a bigger charger.
 For an iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max, the UGREEN Nexode Pro 65W has the 60W-plus output Apple quotes for its fastest charge; check its listing for USB PD 3.2 AVS, which that top speed also depends on.
 If you want one charger for a phone and a laptop, the UGREEN Nexode Pro 65W covers both from a single outlet.
 Do USB-C iPhones need a special charger? No. A USB-C iPhone, which means an iPhone 15, iPhone 16, iPhone 17 or iPhone 18 Pro, uses the same USB Power Delivery standard as every other USB-C device, so any PD charger here works.
 For most iPhones, around 30W is the practical ceiling for fast charging, so a larger charger will not charge them faster; what it gives you is headroom to charge other devices at the same time.
 The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are the exception: Apple quotes up to 50% in around 15 minutes with a 60W-capable adapter or higher, and its support page says the phones use USB Power Delivery 3.2 with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS).
 In an independent test reported by MacRumors, the iPhone 18 Pro Max peaked at about 52W for its first 12 minutes, against a 36W peak for the iPhone 17 Pro Max in ChargerLAB’s test.
 So for those two, pick a charger of 60W or more, such as the UGREEN Nexode Pro 65W, and check its listing for PD 3.2 AVS; a charger without AVS still charges them safely, just more slowly.
 Is a GaN charger a fast charger? Yes. GaN chargers are among the fastest USB-C chargers you can carry, because gallium nitride lets a small block push high wattage safely, and every pick here delivers USB Power Delivery. Pair it with a USB-C to USB-C cable rated for the wattage you need, or the cable becomes the limit rather than the charger.
 Is a GaN charger better than a normal charger? For the same wattage, yes: smaller, lighter and cooler, because gallium nitride switches faster and wastes less energy as heat than silicon. It does not charge a phone any faster; the phone sets the pace over USB Power Delivery. The gain is the size of the block in your bag.
 Do GaN chargers throttle when they get hot? The big ones can. In Tom’s Hardware’s 30 minute test all three 140W chargers cut their output after 15 minutes as they warmed up, and a 100W unit slipped from 99W to 89W. Every charger in the 45 to 68W band held full output for the whole run, which is one more reason a 65W block suits one laptop and a phone.
 Is a GaN charger safe to leave plugged in? A certified one, yes. Look for UL or ETL in the US, UKCA in the UK or CE in the EU, all tested against IEC 62368-1, which covers overheating and fire. The risk sits with unbranded copies that skip the thermal cut-out to hit a low weight.
 What are the disadvantages of GaN chargers? Three. They cost more than a silicon charger of the same wattage. The highest-wattage ones still get hot enough under sustained load to throttle. And the label invites fakes, so an unknown brand at an unusually low weight is a charger to avoid.
 Is it worth buying a GaN charger? Yes, if you travel with a laptop or more than one device. You pay a little more than for a silicon charger of the same wattage and you get a block that is smaller, lighter and cooler, which is exactly what matters in a bag. A phone that never leaves the house is happy on any decent USB-C charger.
 Is it okay to use a 100W charger for a 65W laptop? Yes, completely safe. USB Power Delivery negotiates wattage between charger and laptop, so the charger only delivers what the laptop asks for.  100W or more – 14-inch and 15-inch MacBook Pro, Dell XPS 15, gaming laptops, anything with discrete graphics.
 140W or more – 16-inch MacBook Pro, high-end workstations, or fast-charging multiple laptops simultaneously.
 Most travelers fall into the 65W to 100W range. If you carry a 13-inch laptop and a phone, 65W is enough. If you carry a 14-inch or 15-inch laptop, step up to 100W. Going higher than you need costs money and weight.
 International Plug Compatibility Explained
 Most GaN chargers sold in the US include a US-style Type A or Type B plug. International travel usually requires either a separate plug adapter or a charger with built-in international prongs. The MOMAX and UGREEN 65W Travel Adapter both include switchable plugs that cover multiple countries.
 Voltage compatibility is separate from plug type. Most modern GaN chargers accept 100V to 240V input, which covers North America (110-120V) and Europe/Asia (220-240V). Check the charger’s input voltage rating before assuming it will work overseas. All eight chargers in this guide support universal voltage.
 TSA and Airline Rules for GaN Chargers
 TSA allows GaN chargers in both carry-on and checked luggage. The Federal Aviation Administration does not set watt-hour limits on chargers the way it does for spare laptop batteries. The watt-hour limit applies to battery packs, not the chargers themselves. Pack chargers wherever is convenient.
 Airline policies occasionally call for chargers to be removable from bags during screening. Keep your GaN charger in an easily accessible pocket of your carry-on for faster security lines. International carriers follow similar rules, though enforcement varies by country.
 Safety Features to Look For
 Quality GaN chargers include at least three internal protections: overvoltage protection (OVP), overcurrent protection (OCP), and short-circuit protection (SCP). Higher-end models add thermal monitoring like Anker’s ActiveShield or UGREEN’s PWM chip. These features prevent the most common charging failures.
 Look for third-party safety certifications from UL, FCC, TUV, or CE marks. These indicate independent laboratory testing. All eight chargers in this guide carry at least two of these certifications, which is a baseline I recommend for any charger you put in a bag.
 Frequently Asked Questions About GaN Travel Chargers
 Do GaN chargers work internationally?
 Yes, most GaN chargers accept 100V to 240V input voltage, which covers every major power grid worldwide including North America (110-120V), Europe (220-240V), the UK (230V), and Asia (100-240V). The limitation is the plug type. Chargers sold in the US include Type A or Type B plugs, which fit North American and Japanese outlets. To use a GaN charger in countries with Type C, G, or I outlets (Europe, UK, Australia), you need either a separate plug adapter or a charger with switchable international plugs like the MOMAX 70W Universal or UGREEN 65W Travel Adapter in this guide.
 Are there any drawbacks to GaN chargers?
 GaN chargers have three main drawbacks. First, they cost more than equivalent silicon chargers because Gallium Nitride semiconductors are more expensive to manufacture. Second, the highest-wattage GaN chargers still run warm under sustained load, though cooler than silicon alternatives. Third, early-generation GaN chargers occasionally had reliability issues, but current GaN II and GaN III models from reputable brands have failure rates similar to traditional chargers. For most travelers, the size and weight savings far outweigh these minor trade-offs.
 Are GaN chargers allowed in flight?
 Yes, TSA and the FAA allow GaN chargers in both carry-on and checked luggage. The FAA watt-hour restrictions that apply to spare lithium batteries do not extend to the chargers themselves. GaN chargers contain no batteries, only the AC-to-DC conversion circuitry. Pack your charger in whichever bag is most convenient, though placing it in an accessible pocket of your carry-on speeds up security screening when TSA asks you to remove electronics.
 Who makes the best GaN charger?
 Anker, UGREEN, Baseus, and Satechi are the most reputable GaN charger brands based on user reviews and reliability data. Anker dominates the premium tier with the Nano II, Prime, and GaNPrime lines. UGREEN wins on value with the Nexode series. Baseus offers competitively priced options in the budget range. Satechi focuses on design-conscious MacBook users. For travel specifically, the Anker Prime 100W and UGREEN Nexode 100W are the two strongest picks based on testing data from multiple review sites including ZDNet, The Gadgeteer, and Smart Gear Outlet.
 Final Verdict: Best GaN Chargers for Travel in 2026
 After 90 days of testing, the Anker Prime 100W remains my top pick for the best GaN chargers for travel. It pairs genuine 100W output with a compact foldable design, premium build quality, and proven long-term reliability across business trips from New York to Tokyo.
 If you need more ports or want to save money, the UGREEN Nexode 100W delivers four ports and over 11,000 positive reviews at a lower cost. International travelers should add the MOMAX 70W Universal to their bag for switchable plugs across 224+ countries. Pick the model that matches your device list and travel style, and your carry-on will thank you.

 UGREEN bundles three plug heads in the box alongside a quick start guide. There is no USB-C cable, so you will need to supply your own. The heads clip on with a satisfying click and release through a small button, which is easier than unscrewing adapters on older travel chargers.

 The front carries two USB-C ports and one USB-A port. The button on the back releases the attached plug head, and a small recess stores the US head when it is swapped out. Build quality is solid; there is no wobble between the body and a fitted head.

 A single-region 65W charger is smaller and lighter, no question. But when you land in a different country you still need a plug adapter, and that is extra weight and bulk in your bag.
 The Nexode carries US, UK and EU heads in the box and switches between them without tools. If you only ever charge at home, the size penalty makes no sense. If you cross regions even once or twice a year, leaving the separate adapter at home is the point.

 Independent testing
 UGREEN Nexode 65W review: charging performance

 45W + 20W split
 Documented the two-USB-C split as 45W plus 20W, and saw an occasional secondary-port drop below 45W while charging a Steam Deck, fixed by re-seating the cable.

 Under an hour each
 Recharged an Asus ROG Ally and a Surface Pro X in under an hour each from the Nexode 65W over a single USB-C connection.

 The 65W rating is UGREEN’s own number, but Digital Camera World confirmed each port reaches its advertised speed on its own, and Windows Central’s recharge times on two demanding devices are exactly what a healthy 65W charger should produce. For one laptop, tablet or large handheld at a time, there is no asterisk.
 Share it between devices and the arithmetic takes over. The 65W budget divides rather than stretches: iMore’s documented splits leave the first port 45W at most once anything else is drawing power, and Digital Camera World found a MacBook could not stay topped up on a full three-port load, which is what 45W does to a big laptop that is working hard. Give the laptop the first port and let phones and earbuds take the leftovers.
 One quirk is worth knowing before a trip: iMore saw the secondary port occasionally dip while feeding a Steam Deck, and re-seating the cable cured it. If a device seems slow on the second port, try the cable before blaming the charger.
 No independent outlet recorded sustained thermal or efficiency numbers we could verify, so we are not quoting them. What we can say is that the charger runs warm under a full load, which is normal for a 65W GaN unit of this size.
 Darleene’s version: If you charge one laptop or one big tablet, this is fast. If you charge three things at once, the big device slows down to 45W, which is enough to keep going but not enough to recover quickly.

 With all three ports occupied the split becomes 45W plus 8.5W plus 8.5W.  At 340g the Nexode is heavier than a plain 65W GaN charger, and its 65mm square face takes up more room in a bag. The fair comparison is not against a single-region charger but against a single-region charger plus a separate travel adapter.

You need to keep your phone and other devices charged, regardless of where you're going, why, and however long for. I myself am a frequent flier, and my packing checklist is incomplete without my favorite 70W universal adapter from Baseus. It packs plenty of power and has many ports. Plus there's a built-in USB-C cable in case I forget mine or need a spare.
 A powerful USB adapter is an absolute must-have for several reasons. Firstly, you're never guaranteed to find the right plugs that match your current primary USB-C charger . And secondly, you have limited space when traveling so it's necessary to carry only one charger that works with all your tech.
 This is why I suggest grabbing a travel adapter with multiple combinations of USB ports and a very high wattage so everything from your phone to your laptop can connect to it. If you're seeking the best USB adapter for travel, I've curated this guide based on these criteria.

Things like power banks and audio accessories don't need a separate charging cable or charger from your phone if it's all USB-C. Most modern laptops support USB-C charging as well, but they need 65W or higher charging speeds.

The high power rating means you can plug in multiple things in one go and still get the fastest charging speed on every device.
